To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Levin’s verb classes can be automatically acquired from corpora with reasonable accuracy, 2) the best-performing features are based on dependency information and co-occurrence information, 3) subcategorization frame information is not as useful as one would expect from a theoretical perspective, and 4) the Levin classes, while useful, are not as useful as we would expect from a practical perspective.
the best features for automatic verb classifications are based on co-occurrence and dependency information, and that the best performing classifier uses a combination of these features.
(a) Levin’s classes are a useful basis for classification, and (b) dependency information and simple collocation information are more useful than subcategorization information.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the empirical basis for the Levin verb classification, and the relation between Levin-style verb classification and automatic verb classification.
the question of how best to represent verbs for automatic classification.

a fundamental issue in computational linguistics: what are the best features for a given task? We have found a surprising answer: the best features for verb classification are not the most theoretically motivated ones, but rather the most empirically motivated ones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, although Levin’s classification is an important step towards a more principled and theoretically motivated description of verb semantics, it is not yet a complete and fully satisfactory account.
Levin’s classification is not the most effective way for automatic verb classification, although it is a very good starting point.
Levin’s classes are useful for the purpose of reducing redundancy, but they are not useful for the purpose for which they were intended, that is, for the purpose of predicting the behavior of verbs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best-performers are not the features that are most theoretically motivated, but the features that best capture the distributional patterns of verbs in the corpus.
the Levin-style verb classification is a good starting point but that the best results will be achieved by combining Levin’s approach with a broader set of features.

Levin’s approach is not the best way to acquire verb classes from corpora, but that her work is an important starting point for a more comprehensive and more empirically based approach to verb classification.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the theoretical basis of Levin’s work does not always translate well into effective feature sets for automatic classification.
Levin’s approach to verb classification, while theoretically motivated, is not necessarily the optimal approach for automatic classification.
the Levin classes are not as useful as they are often claimed to be for automatic verb classification tasks.
